paragraphs: I would fulfill the purpose of this book only imperfectly if, having shown what opinions and feelings the principle of equality suggests, I did not point out before concluding the general influence these same opinions and feelings may have on the government of human societies. To succeed in this I will often have to retrace my steps. But I trust the reader will not refuse to follow me along paths already familiar to him, which may lead to some new truth.

The principle of equality makes men independent of each other, and gives them a habit and a taste for following no other guide than their own will in their private actions. They constantly enjoy this complete independence toward their equals and in the dealings of private life. It tends to make them look on all authority with a jealous eye, and it soon suggests to them the idea and the love of political freedom. Men living in such times have a natural bent toward free institutions. Take any one of them at random and search, if you can, his deepest instincts. You will find that of all governments, the one he will most quickly conceive and most highly value is the one whose head he has himself elected and whose administration he can control. Of all the political effects produced by equality of conditions, this love of independence is the first to strike the observer and to alarm the timid. Nor can it be said that their alarm is entirely misplaced, for anarchy looks more formidable in democratic countries than elsewhere. The citizens have no direct influence on each other. So as soon as the supreme power of the nation fails, the power that kept them all in their several stations, it would seem that disorder must instantly reach its extreme, that every man would draw off in a different direction, and that the fabric of society must at once crumble away.

I am nevertheless convinced that anarchy is not the principal evil that democratic ages have to fear, but the least. For the principle of equality gives rise to two tendencies. One leads men straight to independence and may suddenly drive them into anarchy. The other leads them by a longer, more secret, but more certain road to servitude. Nations readily see the first tendency and are prepared to resist it; they are carried along by the second without seeing where it leads. It is therefore especially important to point it out. For my part, I am so far from reproaching the principle of equality for making men hard to manage that this very circumstance chiefly earns my approval. I admire the way it places in the mind and heart of man a dim conception and an instinctive love of political independence, and so prepares the remedy for the evil it produces. It is for this very reason that I am attached to it.
